BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: As the upper trough continues steering out east across our area on Friday, valley rain and mountain snow will continue in the morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Eastward moving cold front will continue valley rain and mountain snow over southwest/west-central ID this morning through evening.
- Brief drying period tonight through early Wednesday, then another Pacific storm late Wednesday through Thursday, bringing a cooler and windier pattern. Not as wet as current storm.
- Another Pacific storm returning precip chances late Saturday through early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The cold front currently steering across our area will continue widespread valley rain and mountain snow on the western ID side this morning through tonight. The precipitation band will taper off east later in the afternoon today, before completely moving out of our area by late tonight. This frontal passage will be followed immediately by a brief ridge of high pressure building over the area, bringing a dry break this evening through Wednesday morning.

From Wednesday through Thursday, a deep Pacific upper low will sweep into the northwest and Great Basin, returning a swath of precipitation and a cooling trend across the area. Elevated wind gusts are expected Wednesday with this second system, with stronger gusts over 30 mph in higher terrain areas and the upper Treasure Valley through Magic Valley. Snow levels will mostly hang in the 3500-4500 ft range from today through late week, but are expected to temporarily drop to valley floors overnight Tuesday through early Wednesday. As such, widespread snow showers are expected across eastern OR Wednesday morning, but with accumulations between 0.5-1 inches for lower-elevation areas. The lower Treasure Valley, mainly on the east OR side, can see rain/snow mixes or dusting of snow in the morning hours of Wednesday, before snow levels climb back up to the 3500-4500 ft range by the evening. Thursday will see continuous valley rain and mountain snow as the upper trough steers directly over our area, but the overall intensity of precipitation will lower down by late Thursday. Total precipitation expected from this second system will remain on the lower side, with valleys generally seeing total rain accumulations less than 0.20 inches. Higher terrain areas on both the west-central ID and eastern OR sides will likely see 2 to 4 inches of total snow accumulations, with up to 5-7 inches limited to high peaks, by early Friday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: As the upper trough continues steering out east across our area on Friday, valley rain and mountain snow will continue in the morning. With snow levels expected to briefly drop to valley floors in the early hours, valleys may see a rain/snow mix Friday morning. Precipitation will completely taper off by late Friday/early Saturday as the system moves out of our area. A brief ridge will build into the area early Saturday, returning a short dry break before another Pacific upper trough digs into the northwest region late Saturday. The area will see slight to moderate chances of precipitation late Saturday through early Sunday. But come late Sunday, there is considerable guidance uncertainty over how much precipitation the area will receive as the trough digs down into California and the Great Basin. For now, higher terrain areas will see the higher chances of precipitation late Sunday through early Tuesday. Temperatures will hover near or slightly below normal throughout the long term period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Beyond that storm system, guidance does indicate a fairly active storm track across the western CONUS, with chances for light precipitation (mainly over the mountains) every few days.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Locally dense fog across the plains this morning, mainly in Weld and Morgan counties.
- First wind event of the season likely for the northern Front Range mountains and foothills Tuesday night into Wednesday. A few gusts up to 75 mph plausible.
- Elevated or near-critical fire weather conditions possible across the Denver metro and Palmer Divide Wednesday afternoon.
- Chances for mountain snow late Tuesday night into Wednesday morning. Another event likely Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: We're starting to see stratus and fog increase again across portions of the northeast plains tonight, with some patchy dense fog noted near the edge of the stratus deck in Weld county. Guidance again favors fog across the Poudre/South Platte River valleys east of I-25 late tonight into the mid-morning hours. There's some signals we could get dense fog again across Weld/Morgan/Logan counties but will punt a decision on Dense Fog Advisories for a couple hours longer.

Tuesday should be another warm and dry day across the forecast area, with southwesterly flow aloft increasing through the day ahead of a sharp shortwave. That shortwave is expected to push through/north of the region Tuesday night, before quickly lifting into the Dakotas by Wednesday afternoon.

Guidance produces a well-defined area of rain and snow across Utah during the day Tuesday - associated with the mid-level trough/front - which quickly advances into the western fringes of our CWA late Tuesday evening. High resolution guidance continues to be more bullish with the eastward extent of precip/snow with this wave, producing a few inches of snow across the Park Range and an inch or so for most of the central/northern mountains overnight. Steep lapse rates and mid-level frontogenesis, along with 0-2km mean winds near 30-35kt would favor some convective/snow squall like structures across the northern mountains that could produce some briefly moderate/heavy snow before moisture quickly dries up overnight. Models also hold on to a little bit of additional light snow for the Park Range Wednesday morning before completely drying out the boundary layer after noon.

While the snow is a welcome arrival, this system will also produce quite a bit of wind for the Front Range. Cross-barrier flow increases to around 50kt Wednesday morning in a substantially subsident regime between 800-500mb. Both the RRFS and HRRR continue to advertise >60kt gusts across northern Front Range mountains and higher foothills, and I don't see a reason to make any changes to the existing High Wind Watch at this time. The main question at this point is if any of these stronger mountain wave winds make it into the I-25 corridor before the wave breaks down. There is not a clear signal with tonight's guidance, but there is good agreement that the flow will weaken Wednesday afternoon leading to some gusty but not significantly strong winds across the I-25 corridor and plains. The main concern there will be fire weather - see the section further below for additional discussion.

Thursday looks to be a quieter day across the region in between storm systems. Temperatures should moderate a bit across the higher elevations with highs remaining in the low to mid 50s across the plains.

The end of week system still looks to take a more favorable track for snow across the higher elevations. A broad upper low is expected to transition back to an open wave as it approaches the region, with a couple of shortwaves moving through Colorado as they rotate around the base of the trough. This leaves most of the higher elevations in a broad, moist west-southwesterly flow aloft for about 24-36 hours from Friday through Saturday before the final shortwave lifts out of the region during the day Saturday. Of course, a WSW direction is still modestly unfavorable for a lot of our terrain, but the longer duration of this event would at least provide a few inches for most of our mountains. While the day shift was (understandably) bearish about any chances for precipitation across the plains, it was interesting to see the GFS/ECMWF/ICON all throw some light QPF across some of the lower elevations early Saturday, with a slightly more favorable look at 500mb. Given what looks to be a low predictability synoptic setup across the west, I suppose this period is worth watching if you're desperate to see some flakes fly east of the divide.

Beyond that storm system, guidance does indicate a fairly active storm track across the western CONUS, with chances for light precipitation (mainly over the mountains) every few days. Nothing particularly stands out at this point, but NBM seems to capture the chances for mountain snow well enough.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Precipitation chances will be slim further east, but we can still expect this system to bring a change in the weather as a cold front passes through the High Plains Friday night.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog will persist over portions of the High Plains through Tuesday morning.
- The first notable high wind event of the season is on track Tuesday evening through Wednesday. High Wind Watches and Warnings are in effect.
- Wind gusts of 60 to 75 mph are expected in the typical wind prone areas along Interstates 80 and 25, with gusts up to 60 mph possible in adjacent zones.
- Expect a quick hitting round of rain and snow showers in Carbon and western Albany Counties tonight.
- Another round of snow showers may impact the same areas Thursday night into Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A pattern change is around the corner this morning as active weather returns to the region. Current GOES water vapor channel satellite imagery shows the broad ridge that supported the recent warm temperatures shifting off to our east as the next Pacific trough gradually moves inland. At the surface, a surface trough is positioned just east of the I-25 corridor, with a fairly humid airmass in place to the east. Dewpoints in the mid to upper 30s are present this morning, supporting areas of low clouds and fog in far eastern Wyoming and western Nebraska. Temperatures above seasonal averages are expected again today, but we will see a bit more cloud cover today.

The Pacific trough currently over the inter-mountain west will begin to exert its influence on the area this evening. Persistent southwest flow aloft will support lee cyclogenesis over north central Wyoming by this evening, and then this surface cyclone will drift east-northeast into the Dakotas by midday Wednesday. The cross- barrier pressure gradient will rapidly increase this evening. Gradients peak Wednesday morning, and then gradually decrease Wednesday afternoon. GFS Craig to Casper 700 and 850-mb height gradients are both around 70m to even close to 80m, which easily supports high winds in at least the wind prone areas. Winds aloft begin as SSW to SW this evening, and then transition to WSW to W behind the upper level shortwave trough axis, which passes through the area early Wednesday morning. LREF mean 700-mb winds over the Laramie range continue to push around 60 knots during the peak of the event Wednesday morning. There remains some variability in the ensemble suite, but even the low end scenario now supports high winds, at least for the wind prone areas. In-house guidance has generally held steady as well, showing probabilities around 70% for all of the typical wind prone areas, and probabilities around 40% for adjacent zones including Rawlins, Douglas, and Cheyenne. Therefore, inherited High Wind Watches were all upgraded to High Wind Warnings (though the timing was shifted a touch earlier for both start time and end time), and High Wind Watches were added for Converse county and central Laramie county, including Cheyenne, where confidence remains lower. Expected gradients should support gusts easily 60+ mph for the wind prone areas, with a chance to push closer to 75 mph depending on how the mountain wave setup ends up playing out. On that note, RAP guidance shows a modest stable layer developing a bit above mountain-top height behind the trough axis early Wednesday morning with the strongest winds located roughly inside the inversion. This suggests the possibility for vertically propagating mountain waves and mountain wave breaking activity, which could locally enhance lee-side wind speeds. However, the inversion height is a little high and the mountain wave potential is not a slam dunk. High resolution guidance is somewhat divergent, despite good agreement in the global suite. The HRRR shows fairly widespread high winds, even outside of existing headlines, while the newly operational RRFS keeps high winds mostly confined to the wind prone areas with gusts only around 50 mph in adjacent zones. The HRRR does have a tendency to be a little over-aggressive at this lead time, but not always. On the other hand, the RRFS has not been around long enough to assess its performance during high wind events, so this will be interesting to observe.

While the main story with this shortwave trough is the wind potential, we are also monitoring a quick-hitting precipitation event for portions of Carbon and Albany counties. This evening, ahead of the primary trough axis, the southwest flow aloft will have decent cloud layer moisture. Mechanical forcing driven by rapid pressure rises at the surface with some very weak instability will drive rain and high elevation snow showers pushing into Carbon county around 5PM to 9PM. Drier air works into the cloud layer after that, but widely scattered snow showers will continue over the area through about mid-morning Wednesday. We remain on track for about 2 to 4" of snow in the higher peaks of the Sierra Madre, and perhaps a dusting to an inch or two in the Snowy range. The primary window with the best moisture will likely be too warm for snow at the elevations of the I-80 corridor, but the lingering snow showers after could cause briefly hazardous conditions late this evening into Wednesday morning. Very dry air will work into the area late Wednesday morning through the afternoon, likely shutting off any precipitation and transitioning focus to elevated fire weather conditions over the plains. Rapid cold air advection is expected Wednesday. Laramie and Rawlins will struggle to get to 40 degrees, while areas to the east will be stuck in the 40s to lower 50s with strong, gusty winds making it feel chillier. While this will feel chilly relative to recent weather, expected highs Wednesday do not differ significantly from seasonal averages. Look for winds to weaken Wednesday evening with a chilly night expected.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Wednesday's storm system will be gone as quickly as it moves in, with transient ridging expected to build back into the area on Thursday. Areas west of the Laramie range should easily warm 10F above Wednesday's values, whereas those to the east may be similar to just a few degrees warmer thanks to cool southeast surface winds and cloud cover increasing once again. Attention then shifts to the next shortwave trough moving in from the Pacific, which will start to influence our weather Thursday night. Ensembles are now in excellent agreement depicting this storm system as a largely limited precipitation event, mostly confined to the higher terrain. Nearly all ensemble members have little to no precipitation falling over the High Plains thanks to the upper level low remaining north of the area. The flow aloft remaining southwest Thursday night and much of Friday will also be an unfavorable direction for orographic lift for most of the area (except Carbon county). Spotty moisture in the cloud layer should support on and off snow showers beginning Thursday night and continuing into Friday in Carbon County. While some brief mixing with rain is possible at the onset, this event is expected to be primarily snow. Advisory criteria snowfall amounts are possible in our western areas. The Sierra Madre range has the highest probability (around 60%) for Advisory criteria snowfall, while the Snowy range falls around 30%, and the valleys of Carbon county are around 20%.

Precipitation chances will be slim further east, but we can still expect this system to bring a change in the weather as a cold front passes through the High Plains Friday night. While Carbon, Albany, and Converse counties will be noticeably colder Friday, remaining areas of the High Plains should still manage to reach near or slightly above average high temperatures. Saturday, meanwhile, is expected to be about 5F colder than average across the board. Expect locally breezy to windy conditions, particularly on Friday and Friday night, but the probability for high winds is low at this time (about 20 to 30% for the wind prone areas). While ridging will try to recover behind this system, ensembles are in relatively good agreement on limiting the warm-up Sunday and Monday, with temperatures remaining generally near or even slightly below seasonal averages.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late Thursday night through Saturday morning. Models still show an open wave setup.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - The next system will bring valley rain and mountain snow on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed by another storm system on Friday and Saturday.
- Wind gusts of 25-45 mph will be common Tuesday afternoon and evening.
- Mountain passes could see adverse travel conditions Tuesday night and Wednesday morning due to snow.
- Temperatures will trend downward late week, with colder air delivering the first freezing temperatures for some desert valleys.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: SHOWERS TUESDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY MORNING:

Dry conditions with increasing clouds are expected today. The next system moves across the area Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday morning. Strong southwesterly winds develop Tuesday ahead of the system. Gusts tomorrow could reach 45 mph especially across the southwest half of the area. Showers and perhaps a few embedded thunderstorms develop Tuesday afternoon and continue through Wednesday morning. Rainfall amounts in the valleys are generally under 0.5" with most places seeing a trace-0.25". Snow levels will start around 9-10kft when showers arrive and drop to around 6-7kft overnight. The southern mountains and Utah mountains will be favored for this event. Snowfall amounts above 9kft will range from 4-10" with lesser amounts for lower elevations. The other mountain ranges could expect more like 1-4". Blowing snow and snow packed roads may cause travel impacts on the mountain passes Tuesday night.

Showers will taper off around daybreak Wednesday, as this system exits the region. A few lingering snow showers will continue along the Divide Wednesday morning. Cooler and drier conditions develop on Wednesday with temperatures 10 to 15 degrees colder behind the front. A weak transitory ridge moves overhead Wednesday and Thursday as another more organized system comes ashore out west.

Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late Thursday night through Saturday morning. Models still show an open wave setup. Precipitation totals continue to vary by model run, with the central and northern mountains of Colorado picking up additional snow in the latest runs. Differences among the models with regards to strength and timing keep confidence low attm. Most of the moisture is expected to arrive ahead of the cold front, making timing critical. Snow levels could drop to some valley floors Friday night into Saturday morning. For now, however, the specifics remain uncertain.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Brief upper ridge across the area on Thu will bring dry and mild conditions, then next fast-moving upper trough approaches the area late in the day.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Warmer today most locations, with increasing afternoon winds, especially across the mountains and in the San Luis Valley.
- Quick-moving system will bring brief snow to the mountains (mainly ern San Juans) overnight, with gusty winds all areas tonight into Wed.
- After a dry and mild day Thu, another weather system will bring back strong winds Thursday night through Friday, with mountain snow possible, especially along the Continental Divide.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Patchy fog across the Arkansas Valley from Pueblo eastward early this morning will dissipate quickly today, as southwest winds increase in response to surface pressure falls on the plains ahead of incoming western U.S. upper trough. Max temps today will warm with better mixing, and most valleys/plains will see 50s/60s, with 40s/50s mountains. Continued to hold back temps slightly over the far sern plains, where stratus could linger through the day, keeping maxes down a bit.

Overnight, upper wave whips quickly through the area, with best forcing rapidly shifting into the nrn Rockies by Wed morning. As a result, expect a quick burst of snow showers late this afternoon/early this evening over the ern San Juans, potentially tracking eastward across the remainder of the Continental Divide and San Luis Valley after sunset, before dissipating over the Sangres toward midnight as upward motion ends. Forecast snowfall amounts continue to decrease, with 4-5 inches over the higher peaks of the ern San Juans, and 1-3 inches elsewhere along the Continental Divide/higher peaks of the Sangres. Main feature of the passing trough at most locations will be gusty winds, with gusts 25-45 mph common tonight into Wed, and perhaps some 50-60 mph gusts over the mountains/favored east slopes. Wed maxes cool slightly west of I-25, while well-mixed plains again rise into the 60s as cold advection looks weak to non-existant.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Brief upper ridge across the area on Thu will bring dry and mild conditions, then next fast-moving upper trough approaches the area late in the day. System will spread snow showers to the Continental Divide beginning Thu night, with best window for precip during the day on Fri. System continues to track fairly far north, which will limit precip away from the Divide, though a least a few ensemble members hint at some energy hanging back in the base of the trough late Fri into Sat, which could at least keep some high terrain snow showers going into Sat morning. Accumulating snow again looks heaviest over the ern San Juans (4-6 inches), with lighter amounts (1-3 inches) farther north in the central mountains. Winds will be gusty all locations again during the day Friday into Friday evening, with at least some guidance suggesting gusts over 60 mph spreading from the mountains through the San Luis Valley and southern I-25 corridor late in the day. Bulk of Sat into Sun then looks dry and cool, before showers return early next week as still another trough approaches the region.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The break in the action will be short lived, however, with a somewhat colder system anticipated to move across the area Thursday into Friday bringing the potential for significant snow to the mountains once again, particularly in the Upper Cottonwoods and areas near Brian Head, with light valley snow accumulations looking increasingly likely as well.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - There is a marginal risk for excessive rainfall (level 1 of 4) across southern Utah today, as a strong cold front sweeps through the region.

- Winter Weather Advisories are in effect for the Wasatch, western Uinta, and southern mountains where 4 to 10 inches of snow is expected through tonight with locally higher amounts. A Winter Weather Advisory is also in effect for the Wasatch Back, where 1 to 4 inches of snow is expected. This system also has the potential to bring accumulating snow to some northern Utah valleys, including the Wasatch Front, this evening.

- Another storm system will bring significant mountain snow Thursday into Friday, with snow levels falling near to below 5000 feet by Friday. Another 6 to 12 inches of mountain snow, with locally higher amounts near 2 feet for the upper Cottonwoods and near Brian Head can be expected.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A broad Pacific trough is currently over the Great Basin, with its associated front edge cold front currently over western Utah. This is resulting in an area of rain (snow above 7000 feet) across western Utah that has been steadily translating east with the movement of the trough. This initial band will move into eastern Utah this afternoon, with southern Utah precipitation tending to taper off late this afternoon/early this evening.

With the arrival of the main trough, cold pool instability will bring another round of precipitation, heavy at times, will develop. primarily focused over northern portions of the area. Snow levels will drop rapidly with this round of precipitation to as low as 4000 feet. Overall, temperatures with the trough over Nevada have been running very much on the cold side of guidance, so have tweaked snow levels down for the early evening. With this in mind, accumulating snow is looking increasingly likely for some northern Utah valleys, including the Wasatch Front, though given warm antecedent temperatures, valley floor accumulations will be generally light mainly limited to grassy surfaces, with more widespread accumulations for bench locations.

Snow accumulations will be significant for both the mountains of southern and northern Utah, and have gone ahead and expanded the going Winter Weather Advisory to the Western Uintas given anticipated accumulations and impacts. Across northern Utah, the expected snow could bring some minor travel impacts for the latter half of the Tuesday evening commute in the valleys, with impacts more likely for higher passes such as Parleys Summit.

As the Pacific trough exits, high pressure is expected to quickly move in for Wednesday morning, with the clearing allowing temperatures to drop. It should be noted that SLC airport has not yet gone below freezing this fall, and if anticipated freezing temperatures tonight hold off until after midnight, it will be the latest first fall freeze on record for the site (previous record is 11/17 set in both 2021 and 2016). Dry conditions are then expected to prevail for most of Wednesday, with southerly winds increasing.

The break in the action will be short lived, however, with a somewhat colder system anticipated to move across the area Thursday into Friday bringing the potential for significant snow to the mountains once again, particularly in the Upper Cottonwoods and areas near Brian Head, with light valley snow accumulations looking increasingly likely as well. Another brief return of high pressure is then expected over the weekend. However, with the lack of a blocking ridge developing off the Pacific coast, another storm system is expected to move through the area early next week, with additional systems potentially following thereafter.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe on Tuesday. Monitor afternoon warming. If you find wet snow surfaces, there is potential for small loose avalanches.
On shady slopes the current snowpack surface is weak and faceted. It will not take much new snow by Wednesday morning to make for easily triggered, small avalanches.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Keep an eye on increasing winds and snow transport throughout the day. If you find slightly stiffer, wind-blown drifts on a steeper slope at higher elevations, consider avoiding that terrain. There's a chance you could trigger a small avalanche in an isolated terrain feature.
